draft.title: Intertextual connections and interpretation
card: An intertextual connection is a link between one text and another. It might be a reference, a borrowed plot, a similar character or a retold story.
Spotting a link gives the reader a second text to compare with. The reader can then ask what the new text keeps, changes or challenges.
Structure and devices also shape a reading. For example, a story told in reverse order or a repeated symbol makes the reader look for a pattern or meaning.
Different links and devices can lead to different readings. A good interpretation is backed by evidence from the text.
draft.remember: Links to other texts, and the way a text is built, can change what a reader thinks it means.

a.q: Why does noticing an intertextual connection help a reader interpret a text?
opts: It gives a second text to compare, so new meanings appear
It proves the author copied the earlier text with no ideas
It means the text has only one correct meaning
It lets the reader skip the evidence in the text
a.why: A linked text gives the reader something to compare, so they can see what the new text keeps or changes. A link does not settle one meaning, and a reading still needs evidence from the text.
a.clue: Think about what a second text lets you compare.

b.q: Priya's short story is set in a modern city. A girl leaves breadcrumbs to find her way home, and a forest of tall towers surrounds her. What does the link to the fairy tale Hansel and Gretel most likely add to a reading?
opts: It suggests the city is as dangerous as the fairy tale forest
It shows the story must have a happy ending
It proves the story is a retelling of only that fairy tale
It makes the setting less important to the meaning
b.why: The breadcrumbs and forest echo the fairy tale, so a reader may see the city as a dangerous place where children can get lost. The link does not fix the ending or prove the story is only a retelling.
b.clue: What does the fairy tale forest stand for, and where does the new story place it?

The story may copy the tale, so it adds no new meaning
The city setting may matter less than the tale's plot
b.why: The breadcrumbs and the forest of towers echo the fairy tale, where children get lost in a dangerous forest. So a reader may see the city as a place of danger too.
